title: Ounahi Scores Twice. Morocco End Canada's World Cup on the Fourth of July.
excerpt: Canada were the better team for 45 minutes. Morocco were the better team for the match. A 3-0 loss in Houston ends the co-hosts' best-ever run.
body:
Canada's World Cup dream — the best run in the country's footballing history — ended where it was always likely to: against a team with more talent, more experience, and more composure when it mattered. Morocco dismantled the co-hosts 3-0 at NRG Stadium in Houston on the Fourth of July, advancing to the quarterfinals where they will face France.

Azzedine Ounahi scored twice. Soufiane Rahimi added a third. And Jesse Marsch, in a postgame press conference that will be replayed endlessly across Canadian sports media, declared: "I'd rather be us than them."

## A First Half of Muscle, No Finish

For 45 minutes, Canada were the better side. They pressed Morocco's midfield relentlessly, forced turnovers, and created the sharper chances. Jonathan David tested Yassine Bounou with an early effort. Tani Oluwaseyi forced a point-blank save. Canada had 56 per cent possession in the first half and the crowd — a mix of Moroccan and Canadian supporters, with a healthy sprinkling of NRIs who had driven down from Dallas and Austin for the holiday weekend — sensed an upset was possible.

But Canada could not score. Alphonso Davies, Bayern Munich's superstar left-back and the most recognizable Canadian footballer alive, watched from the bench. His fitness had not recovered in time, and without his surging runs, Canada lacked the cutting edge to convert pressure into goals. Six yellow cards were distributed in a combative opening half. None translated into a breakthrough.

Morocco's star forward Ismael Saibari limped off in the 22nd minute, adding to the sense that Canada had an opening. They did not take it.

## Ounahi Breaks the Dam

Five minutes into the second half, Achraf Hakimi — the PSG defender who has been one of the tournament's outstanding performers — cut a free-kick short instead of sending it into the box. The ball found Ounahi at the edge of the area. Without controlling it, the Girona midfielder swept a first-time shot through a crowd of bodies and past Max Crépeau at the near post.

Canada pushed forward. Cyle Larin was introduced for his physical presence. The crosses came in. Morocco absorbed them with the same defensive discipline that carried them to the 2022 semifinal in Qatar.

Then, in the 82nd minute, Morocco killed the match. Chemsdine Talbi dribbled through midfield with startling ease. Brahim Diaz — Real Madrid's playmaker, operating between the lines — cut inside and laid the ball off to Ounahi. Another first-time finish. Another Crépeau near-post beating. 2-0.

Ounahi became only the third African player in World Cup history to score a brace in a knockout match.

Rahimi, the man who had replaced the injured Saibari, headed against the bar and then accepted another Diaz assist in stoppage time to make it 3-0. The scoreline was harsh on Canada, but the second-half performance was not.

## What It Means for NRIs in Canada

For the roughly 1.8 million Canadians of Indian origin — the country's largest visible minority group — the World Cup has been a source of unexpected civic pride. Many NRIs who had never followed soccer found themselves watching Canada play at NRG Stadium, at BMO Field in Toronto, and in living rooms from Brampton to Surrey. The co-host tag had given the country something to rally around.

Canada earned its first-ever World Cup point, its first World Cup win (1-0 over South Africa in the Round of 32), and its first knockout-stage appearance. That history is real and worth celebrating.

But the gap between Canada and the world's elite remains significant. Morocco, ranked sixth globally, scored with three of five shots — a 60 per cent conversion rate, the best in a World Cup knockout match since at least 1966, according to Opta. Canada had 11 shot attempts and 11 corner kicks, but forced only three saves.

"We were the better team. They made a couple more plays than us," Marsch insisted. "What a privilege our fans have had to root a team on like this — that goes after the game, that doesn't play defensive. I'd rather be us than them."

## Morocco March On

Morocco are now the first African team to reach the quarterfinals at consecutive World Cups. Their campaign four years ago in Qatar — beating Belgium, Spain, and Portugal to reach the semifinals — was one of the greatest underdog stories in football history. This time, they arrived as contenders, not fairy-tale protagonists.

The quarterfinal against France on July 9 in Foxborough is a rematch of the 2022 semifinal, which France won 2-0 on their way to a runners-up finish. Kylian Mbappé, who scored France's winning penalty against Paraguay on the same evening in Philadelphia, leads the Golden Boot race with seven goals — level with Lionel Messi.

For football fans across the diaspora, the next round promises blockbuster matchups: Portugal vs Spain in Dallas on Monday, USA vs Belgium in Seattle on Monday night, Argentina vs Egypt in Atlanta on Tuesday, and Switzerland vs Colombia in Vancouver — where thousands of Indian-Canadian fans are expected to fill BC Place.

*Sources: Sporting News, Fox Sports, USA Today, The Score*
